summary: Defines a metric for the one-way delay of packets across Internet paths. It builds on the IPPM framework in RFC 2330 and makes RFC 2679 obsolete.

eli5.summary: This says how to measure the time a packet takes to get from here to there, in one direction only.

subtitle: A precise definition of what 'one-way delay' means for an Internet packet, and how to sample and summarize it.

tldr.problem: Measuring how long packets take across the Internet needs an agreed definition, so that results from different tools are comparable.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a single-packet delay metric (Type-P-One-way-Delay), a sample of such values taken at Poisson-process times, and statistics such as percentile, median and minimum.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2679 and is an Internet Standard. It also covers clock error, calibration and what to report.

today: RFC 7679 is an Internet Standard (STD 81) and obsoletes RFC 2679. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it in the metadata for this unit.

sections.title: Why Measure One-Way Delay
sections.content:
RFC 7679 defines a metric for the one-way delay of packets across Internet paths. It builds on the IPPM Framework, RFC 2330, and assumes the reader knows it. The document moves from a singleton (one observation) to a sample (a sequence of singletons) to statistics of the sample, and keeps these clearly separate.

One-way delay is useful because some applications perform badly when delay is large, and erratic variation makes real-time applications hard. The minimum value reflects propagation and transmission delay, and values above it indicate congestion on the path.

It is measured one way rather than as a round trip because the forward and reverse paths may differ (asymmetric paths), may have very different queuing, and may have different QoS provisioning. Measuring each direction separately shows which one is congested.
sections.eli5: Going to school and coming home may take different roads and different times. Timing each trip alone tells you which road has the traffic jam.

sections.title: Time and Clocks
sections.content:
Times are measured in seconds (and fractions) relative to UTC. The RFC separates four notions of clock uncertainty taken from the Framework.

Synchronization
How far two clocks agree, for example one host ahead of another by 5.4 msec.
Accuracy
How far a clock agrees with UTC, for example 27.1 msec behind.
Resolution
The smallest unit by which the clock updates, for example 10 msec on an old Unix host.
Skew
How accuracy or synchronization changes over time, for example gaining 1.3 msec per hour.

For delay, only the differences between clock values matter, so accuracy against UTC is not important to the measurement itself; synchronization between source and destination is.
sections.eli5: To time a trip with two watches, the watches must show the same time. If one runs fast, your answer is wrong.

sections.title: The Singleton: Type-P-One-way-Delay
sections.content:
The metric has four parameters: Src and Dst (IP addresses), T (a time) and Tmax (a loss threshold waiting time). Its value is a real number of seconds or an undefined (informally infinite) number.

The delay from Src to Dst at T is dT when Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet at wire time T and Dst received the last bit at wire time T+dT. It is undefined if Dst did not receive the packet within Tmax.

  • If a packet is duplicated, the first non-corrupt copy to arrive sets the delay.
  • If a packet is fragmented and not reassembled, it is deemed lost.
  • A packet that is not standard-formed is deemed lost.
  • Real delays are positive, but a zero or negative value may be useful within a stream.

The text notes that delays are often 100 usec to 10 msec, so clocks must be closely synchronized. GPS can reach within several tens of usec, while ordinary NTP may only reach several msec.
sections.eli5: Start a stopwatch when the first bit leaves and stop it when the last bit arrives. If it never shows up in time, we write 'lost' instead of a number.

sections.title: Methodology and Errors
sections.content:
A typical method has Src and Dst clocks synchronized, a test packet with padding filled with randomized bits (so path compression does not make delay look lower), a timestamp placed in the packet just before sending, and a timestamp taken as soon as possible on receipt. Subtracting the two gives the estimate. If no packet arrives within a reasonable time, Tmax, the delay is undefined.

The RFC lists error sources. Clock-related uncertainty totals Esynch(t) + Rsource + Rdest. The gap between wire time and host time adds Hsource + Hdest. Together the error bound is Esynch(t) + Rsource + Rdest + Hsource + Hdest.

Calibration finds the systematic and random error of the measurement hosts, for example by connecting two hosts back-to-back. At minimum, a bound e should be found so the reported value is within true value plus or minus e at least 95% of the time. Calibration should be done under the same measurement load the hosts will see in the field.
sections.eli5: Before trusting your stopwatch, test it on a trip you know is nearly instant. Whatever time it still shows is its own error.

sections.title: Samples and Statistics
sections.content:
Type-P-One-way-Delay-Poisson-Stream fixes Src, Dst and Type-P, then picks times from a pseudorandom Poisson process of average rate lambda between T0 and Tf. The sample is the sequence of <time, delay> pairs. Poisson sampling is used to avoid self-synchronization and to limit bias, although the RFC says there is no claim that real traffic is Poisson. If lambda is too large the probes perturb the network, and if too small interesting behavior may be missed. Other sampling methods may suit other situations.

Out-of-order arrival must be handled correctly. Statistics are offered mostly as illustration, and undefined values count as infinitely large.

  • Percentile of the dT values; the example stream (100, 110, undefined, 90, 500 msec) has a 50th percentile of 110 msec.
  • Median, which for an even count is the mean of the two central values (105 msec in the second example).
  • Minimum, 90 msec in the example.
  • Inverse-Percentile, now deprecated because of lack of use.
sections.eli5: Instead of timing one trip, time many trips at random moments. Then you can say the fastest, the middle and the slow ones.

sections.title: Reporting and Security
sections.content:
Calibration and context MUST be reported with results: the exact Type-P used, the loss threshold (or method for telling a large delay from loss), and, where possible, calibration error and the path. Systematic error SHOULD be removed if it can be determined.

Measurement is active and injects packets, so parameters MUST be chosen so the extra traffic is trivial; too much can skew results or cause congestion and denial of service. Measurements can also be harmed if routers treat measurement traffic differently, so methods SHOULD reduce the chance that it can be told apart, or if an attacker injects look-alike traffic. Authentication such as digital signatures may help. Results could also be used for reconnaissance and should be guarded.
sections.eli5: Do not flood the road with test cars, or you cause the jam you wanted to measure. And write down exactly how you measured.
